The rest of the profile does not explain why related people would be a salient trigger.

issues.item: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Evaluation' is poorly matched to the rest of the profile. It suggests social/performance shame concerns, but the negative appraisals and memory items do not involve appearance, performance failure, humiliation, or social judgment. This maladaptive strategy appears to address a symptom theme not otherwise represented.

'Avoid Friends' similarly implies socially driven withdrawal, yet the selected appraisals are global despair and alienation rather than fear of specific interpersonal consequences, and the trigger set does not include friendship or social contact themes. It is not impossible, but in combination with 'Avoid Evaluation' it pulls toward a social-evaluative formulation not supported elsewhere.

For a natural-disaster trauma in a Navy officer, 'Similar cars' is hard to connect clinically to the rest of the profile. The other triggers are generic situational reminders (crowding, locations), but this item implies a specific vehicle-related cue that is not supported by the trauma type, memory content, or appraisals.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: The negative appraisals are extremely global and severe ('life not worth living', 'belong nowhere') relative to the rest of the selected items, which focus on trauma reminders, fragmented imagery, and avoidance. This creates a coherence problem because the profile lacks corresponding threat content or broader self-concept material to support such pervasive suicidal/existential beliefs.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere
issues.explanation: 'I no longer belong anywhere' is especially difficult to reconcile with the demographic/contextual profile of a married Navy officer after a natural disaster unless other items indicate moral injury, social alienation, or occupational rupture; none are present in the selected components.

Clinical Vignette: Commander James Mitchell

Commander James Mitchell was thirty-four when Hurricane Katrina made landfall near the naval base where he was stationed. He had been in the communications center that night, a windowless room deep in the compound, when the storm surge overwhelmed the generators. The backup systems failed in sequence-a sound like industrial machinery screaming, then darkness so complete it seemed to have weight. Water rose through the ventilation shafts. He remembered the smell of it, brackish and chemical, mixed with diesel fuel from the backup tanks. He remembered the cold, the disorientation, the way his hand found the shoulder of the ensign beside him and held on. Twenty-three minutes before power was restored. Twenty-three minutes that had somehow remade him into someone else.

That was eleven years ago. James had remained in the Navy, had married his college sweetheart Rebecca, had built what looked like a stable life. But in the past two years, something had shifted. The triggers had multiplied and tightened around him like a net. Crowded spaces-the commissary, the gym, even the officer's club during social events-sent him into a state of high alert that felt inexplicable to anyone watching him stand rigid in a room full of colleagues. The smell of alcohol, particularly bourbon, would transport him instantly back to that flooded room; he had come to believe, without fully knowing why, that the chemical smell of the floodwater and spilled fuel had mingled with the scent of liquor someone had knocked over in the chaos. Physical locations that resembled the communications center-any windowless, enclosed space-became unbearable. When his wife suggested they see a movie, he found himself unable to enter the darkened theater. The darkness itself was a trigger now, one that made his chest tighten and his mind flood with fragmented images of that night.

These triggers activated a cycle that James had come to depend on, even as it destroyed him. When he found himself in a crowded situation, the visceral memories would surface-his body would involuntarily tense into the same posture he had held in that center, shoulders hunched, muscles locked, as if bracing against the rising water. The memory itself felt unreal, too extreme, a nightmare that couldn't possibly have happened to him. Yet the bodily response was unmistakable. And in response to both the trigger and the memory, James had developed a set of strategies that made sense to him in the moment but had quietly dismantled his life. He began avoiding friends, declining invitations, telling Rebecca he was too tired for social events. He stopped going to the base gym during normal hours, started running alone at dawn. He told himself he deserved this isolation, that what happened that night was somehow his fault-that he should have done more, known more, prevented something he had no power to prevent. The punishment thinking had become a kind of penance. He deserved to suffer because he had survived and others had not, because he had panicked, because he was weak.

The more James isolated himself, the more his negative appraisals hardened into certainty. He had been a gregarious man once, someone who thrived on camaraderie and the structured social life of the military. Now he was always miserable, always aware of a hollow ache in his chest. He no longer belonged anywhere-not in crowded rooms, not in the Navy that had been his identity, not even at home with Rebecca, who increasingly looked at him with a mixture of concern and confusion. This sense of isolation and alienation fed back into his memory. The more he believed he was set apart, the more the memories intruded, and the more the memories intruded, the more he was convinced that certain places and situations would trigger them. His wife had finally insisted he seek help after finding him sitting in their car in the driveway at 2 a.m., unable to go inside because the house was dark. He had been drinking bourbon-something he had never done before-and when she asked him why, he couldn't articulate the strange logic that had driven him to confront the smell, to punish himself with it. James arrived at the clinic carrying a weight of shame and the conviction that he was irreparably broken, that the man he used to be had drowned in that communications center and never come back.
